analogy.p: The **nervous system** is like a **telephone call**: the message goes along a dedicated wire (the neurone), arrives almost at once, and ends when the call is finished. The **endocrine system** is like a **letter posted through the postal network**: the message is put into the delivery system (the **blood**), is carried to every address in the country, and takes longer to arrive, but only the person it is addressed to (the **target organ** with the right **receptors**) opens and acts on it, and the letter can sit there and be read for a long time. The analogy breaks down because a letter is read once and thrown away, whereas a hormone is broken down by the body after it has acted and the effect can be repeated by releasing more.

bullets: **Endocrine system** = a set of **glands** that make and release **hormones**.
Hormones are secreted **directly into the bloodstream** (not through tubes) and carried to a **target organ**.
Compared with the nervous system, the effects are **slower but act for longer**.
The **pituitary gland** is the **'master gland'**: it secretes several hormones in response to body conditions, and these act on other glands.
You must be able to **identify the position** of: pituitary gland, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal gland, ovary and testes.
Typical marks: **1 mark** to name a gland or give its position, **2 to 4 marks** to compare the nervous and endocrine systems, and **4 to 6 marks** in extended answers using several glands.
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: AQA expects you to know that the **endocrine system** is made up of **glands** that **secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream**. The blood carries each hormone to a **target organ**, where it produces an effect. You must be able to compare this with the nervous system: hormonal effects are **slower** but **act for longer**. You must also know that the **pituitary gland** is the **'master gland'**, and be able to **identify the positions** of the **pituitary gland, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal gland, ovary and testes** on a diagram of the human body. This is the foundation for every later topic on hormones, including blood glucose, reproduction and negative feedback.

bullets: **Endocrine gland** = secretes hormones **directly into the blood**.
The hormones are then **carried around the whole body** by the blood plasma.
The main endocrine glands in the specification are the **pituitary, thyroid, adrenal glands, pancreas, ovaries and testes**.
The pancreas is **both** a digestive organ (enzymes) **and** an endocrine gland (insulin and glucagon).
Glands that use ducts (for example salivary glands) release substances to a particular place, not into the blood.
Link to other topics: the same blood that carries oxygen and glucose also carries hormones, so the circulatory system links to hormonal control.
core.h: The endocrine system: glands that secrete hormones
core.p: A **gland** is an organ that makes and releases a useful substance. **Endocrine glands** release their product, a **hormone**, **directly into the bloodstream**. Together these glands form the **endocrine system**. Some glands, such as the sweat glands and salivary glands, release their products through tubes (ducts) onto a surface, so they are not part of the endocrine system. The pancreas is a useful example because it does both jobs: it makes **digestive enzymes** that travel through a duct into the small intestine and it makes **hormones** that go straight into the blood.

bullets: A hormone is a **chemical messenger** carried in the **blood**.
The **target organ** is the organ where the hormone produces its effect.
The target cells have **receptors** that fit the hormone, like a key fitting a lock.
Cells without the matching receptors **do not respond**, even though the hormone passes them.
Each hormone has its own effect, such as **lowering blood glucose** (insulin) or **speeding up the heart** (adrenaline).
Hormones are removed and broken down after use, so their effects are not permanent.
Hormones travel in the **blood plasma**, not along nerves.
core.p: A **hormone** is a **chemical messenger** produced by an endocrine gland and carried in the **blood** to a **target organ**. Only a very small amount of a hormone is needed to cause a response. The target organ is the organ where the hormone has its effect, and it responds because its cells have **receptors** that match that particular hormone. Cells without the matching receptors do not respond, which is why a hormone that travels all around the body only affects its **target organ(s)**. After they have done their job, hormones are removed from the blood and broken down, so the effect can be switched off.

bullets: **Step 1:** a change in the body (stimulus) causes an **endocrine gland** to **secrete a hormone**.
**Step 2:** the hormone passes **directly into the bloodstream**.
**Step 3:** the **blood carries** the hormone to all parts of the body.
**Step 4:** the hormone reaches the **target organ**, where it binds to **receptors** on the target cells.
**Step 5:** the target organ produces a **response** (for example more heat is released, or glucose is taken up).
**Step 6:** the hormone is later broken down and the response stops.
Use the words **secrete, bloodstream, target organ, response** for full marks.
core.h: How hormonal communication works, step by step
core.p: Hormonal control always follows the same sequence of events. A **stimulus** (a change in the body or environment) causes an endocrine gland to release its hormone. The hormone enters the **bloodstream** and is carried round the body. When it reaches its **target organ**, it binds to receptors on the cells there and causes a **response**. Because the hormone has to be carried by the blood, it takes time to arrive, and because it stays in the blood until it is broken down, it can have a long-lasting effect. You should be able to describe this sequence in the right order and use the correct words.

bullets: **Slower** because the hormone has to travel in the **blood** (a transport system) rather than along a neurone.
**Longer-lasting** because the hormone **remains in the blood** until it is broken down.
Some hormonal effects take **days or years**, for example the changes of **puberty** and **growth**.
Many hormones act **throughout the body**, so their effects are more widespread than a nerve impulse.
Nerve impulses are used when a **fast, short-lived** response is needed, such as a reflex.
Link to other topics: this is why your heart keeps racing for a while after a fright (adrenaline stays in the blood).
core.h: Why hormone effects are slower but last longer
core.p: The specification states that, compared with the nervous system, the **effects of hormones are slower but act for longer**. They are slower because the hormone must be **released, carried round the body in the blood** and then **bind to its target cells**, which takes seconds to minutes. A nerve impulse, in contrast, races along a neurone almost instantly. They act for longer because hormones **stay in the blood** until they are broken down or removed, so the response continues, sometimes for hours, days or even years in the case of growth and puberty.

bullets: **Signal:** nervous = electrical impulses; endocrine = chemical hormones.
**Route:** nervous = neurones; endocrine = bloodstream.
**Speed:** nervous = very fast; endocrine = slower.
**Duration:** nervous = short-lived; endocrine = longer-lasting.
**Target:** nervous = specific muscles or glands; endocrine = target organs, often more widespread.
**Example:** nervous = reflex action; endocrine = insulin controlling blood glucose.
Always give **both sides** in a comparison: 'nerves are fast whereas hormones are slower'.
core.h: Comparing the nervous system and the endocrine system
core.p: You will often be asked to compare the two coordination systems. The **nervous system** uses **electrical impulses** that travel along **neurones**, and it produces **fast, short-lived** responses in specific **muscles or glands**. The **endocrine system** uses **chemical hormones** carried in the **blood**, and it produces **slower** but **longer-lasting** effects, often on several organs at once. A good comparison uses a linking word such as 'whereas' and compares the **same feature** for both systems every time.

bullets: **Nervous system:** quick, precise, short-lived responses (reflexes, movement).
**Endocrine system:** slower, longer-lasting, body-wide control (growth, puberty, blood glucose).
Both are needed for **coordination**, which keeps conditions in the body suitable (homeostasis).
Fright example: nerves give an **instant reaction**; **adrenaline** then keeps the heart rate high for longer.
Exam links: this is the basis for **homeostasis**, the **menstrual cycle** and **negative feedback**.
Never say one system is 'better': say which is **more suitable** for the situation and why.
core.h: Why do we need both systems?
core.p: The two systems work together and each is suited to a different kind of job. Where a **rapid response** is needed, such as pulling your hand away from something hot, the **nervous system** is used. Where a **slower, longer-lasting or body-wide change** is needed, such as controlling blood glucose, growth or the menstrual cycle, the **endocrine system** is used. In many situations they act together. For example, when you are frightened, nerves give an immediate reaction and the **adrenal glands** release **adrenaline**, which keeps the body ready for action for longer.

bullets: Position: **base of the brain**, inside the head.
Called the **master gland** because it controls the release of hormones from **other glands**.
It secretes **several hormones** in response to **conditions in the body**.
**ADH** from the pituitary acts on the **kidneys** to control how much water is reabsorbed.
**FSH and LH** from the pituitary act on the **ovaries** in the menstrual cycle (FSH matures an egg and LH causes the egg to be released).
The pituitary also makes **growth hormone** (an extra detail beyond the specification wording).
Link to other topics: ADH links to **water balance**; FSH and LH link to the **menstrual cycle**.
core.p: The **pituitary gland** is a small gland at the **base of the brain**. It is called the **'master gland'** because it **secretes several hormones into the blood in response to body conditions**, and these hormones in turn **act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released**. In this way the pituitary helps to control the activity of many other parts of the endocrine system. For example, the pituitary hormones **FSH and LH** act on the **ovaries** and the hormone **ADH** acts on the **kidneys**. The pituitary itself is controlled by the brain.

bullets: Position: **below the stomach** (behind and below it), in the abdomen.
Hormones: **insulin** and **glucagon**.
These **control blood glucose concentration**.
**Insulin** lowers blood glucose; **glucagon** raises it (detail in blood glucose notes).
It also makes **digestive enzymes** released into the small intestine through a duct.
Diabetes is linked to a problem with insulin (see the blood glucose point).
Link to other topics: **digestion** (enzymes) and **diabetes** (hormone control).
core.p: The **pancreas** is an organ **below and behind the stomach**. As an endocrine gland it secretes the hormones **insulin** and **glucagon**, which control the **concentration of glucose in the blood**. It also makes digestive enzymes (**amylase, protease and lipase**) that are released through a duct into the small intestine, so it has both an endocrine and a digestive role. The detail of how insulin and glucagon work, and what goes wrong in diabetes, is covered in the next specification point on blood glucose.

bullets: Position: **in the neck**, in front of the windpipe.
Hormone: **thyroxine**.
Thyroxine **stimulates the basal metabolic rate** (how fast the body uses energy at rest).
It plays an important role in **growth and development**.
Too little thyroxine can make a person tired and gain weight; too much can speed up the body (extension).
Its level is controlled by **negative feedback** (more detail in the negative feedback point).
Link to other topics: **respiration** and metabolism (energy release).
core.p: The **thyroid gland** is found in the **neck**, in front of the windpipe. It secretes the hormone **thyroxine**. Thyroxine **stimulates the basal metabolic rate**, which is the rate at which the body's cells carry out the chemical reactions of metabolism, and it plays an important role in **growth and development**. The amount of thyroxine in the blood is kept steady by **negative feedback**, which you meet in more detail later in the course.

bullets: Position: **on top of the kidneys** (one on each side).
Hormone: **adrenaline**.
Released in times of **fear or stress**.
**Prepares the body for flight or fight**.
**Increases the heart rate**.
**Boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose** to the **brain and muscles**.
Links to the nervous system: nerves give an instant reaction and adrenaline then maintains the response.
core.p: The **adrenal glands** are a pair of small glands that sit **on top of the kidneys**. They secrete the hormone **adrenaline** in times of **fear or stress**. Adrenaline prepares the body for **'fight or flight'**: it **increases the heart rate** and **boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles**, so that the body is ready for vigorous activity. Adrenaline acts quickly compared with most hormones, but it is still a chemical carried in the blood.

bullets: **Ovaries:** in the **lower abdomen**; secrete **oestrogen** and **progesterone**.
**Oestrogen** is the main female reproductive hormone, involved in **puberty** and the menstrual cycle.
**Testes:** in the **scrotum**; secrete **testosterone**.
**Testosterone** is the main male reproductive hormone and **stimulates sperm production**.
The ovaries are controlled by **FSH and LH** from the pituitary (the master gland).
Do not swap them: oestrogen = ovaries, testosterone = testes.
Link to other topics: **reproduction**, **contraception** and **infertility treatment**.
core.p: The **ovaries** (in females) and **testes** (in males) are endocrine glands as well as organs that make **gametes**. The **ovaries** are in the **lower abdomen**, one on each side of the uterus, and they secrete **oestrogen** (and **progesterone**), which control the menstrual cycle and the female sex characteristics at puberty. The **testes** are in the **scrotum**, outside the abdomen, and they secrete **testosterone**, the main male reproductive hormone, which **stimulates sperm production**. FSH and LH from the pituitary control the ovaries.

bullets: **Pituitary gland:** at the **base of the brain**, in the head.
**Thyroid gland:** in the **neck**, in front of the windpipe.
**Adrenal glands:** one **on top of each kidney**, towards the back of the abdomen.
**Pancreas:** **below and behind the stomach**, in the upper abdomen.
**Ovaries:** **lower abdomen**, either side of the uterus (female).
**Testes:** in the **scrotum**, outside the abdomen (male).
Tip: work from top to bottom: head (pituitary), neck (thyroid), abdomen (adrenals, pancreas), pelvis (ovaries), scrotum (testes).
core.h: Locating the glands on a diagram of the human body
core.p: Examiners can give you a blank diagram of the body and ask you to **identify the position** of a gland, or to label one that is marked with a letter. Learn where each gland is in relation to other organs, because this is much easier to recall than a list. Always check whether the diagram shows a male or a female body, as this decides whether you expect to see ovaries or testes.

bullets: **Gland → hormone → blood → target organ → effect** is the pattern to use.
**Blood glucose:** pancreas (insulin and glucagon).
**Metabolic rate and growth:** thyroid (thyroxine).
**Fear or stress:** adrenal glands (adrenaline).
**Reproduction:** ovaries (oestrogen, progesterone), testes (testosterone), controlled by pituitary hormones FSH and LH.
**Water balance:** pituitary (ADH) acting on the kidneys.
**Negative feedback (Biology only):** hormone levels are kept steady by feedback loops involving the endocrine system.
Higher tier thinking: explain why a hormone only affects its target organ (matching receptors) and why a hormonal response is slower than a nervous one.
core.h: Putting it together: summary and links to other topics
core.p: The endocrine system uses glands to release hormones into the blood, which carry messages to target organs. Each gland has its own hormone or hormones: the **pituitary** (several, including ADH, FSH and LH), the **pancreas** (insulin and glucagon), the **thyroid** (thyroxine), the **adrenal glands** (adrenaline), the **ovaries** (oestrogen and progesterone) and the **testes** (testosterone). This topic is the foundation for blood glucose control, water balance, the menstrual cycle and negative feedback, so a firm grasp now will help with many later questions. Always connect the gland, the hormone, the target organ and the effect.

exam: **State what a hormone is (2 marks):** a chemical messenger (1) secreted by a gland into the blood and carried to a target organ (1).

**Compare nervous and hormonal control (4 marks):** use 'whereas' and compare the same feature each time: electrical impulses v chemical hormones; neurones v blood; fast v slower; short-lived v longer-lasting.
**Name the gland (1 mark):** learn the pairs: pituitary (master gland), pancreas (insulin and glucagon), thyroid (thyroxine), adrenal (adrenaline), ovary (oestrogen), testis (testosterone).
**Identify a position on a diagram (1 mark):** use the organ landmarks: pituitary at the base of the brain, thyroid in the neck, adrenals on top of the kidneys, pancreas below the stomach.

**Explain why the pituitary is called the master gland (2 marks):** it secretes several hormones in response to body conditions (1) which act on other glands to stimulate the release of other hormones (1).

**Explain why a hormone only affects its target organ (2 to 3 marks):** the hormone is carried in the blood to all parts of the body (1) but only the target organ has receptors with a matching shape (1), so only that organ responds (1).

**Explain why hormonal responses are slower (2 marks):** the hormone is secreted into the blood and has to be carried to the target organ (1) rather than travelling along neurones as fast electrical impulses (1).

**Application question (4 marks):** for a frightening situation, say nerves give an immediate response, adrenal glands release adrenaline into the blood, adrenaline increases heart rate and delivers more oxygen and glucose to muscles, and the effects last longer.

**Command words:** 'State' = short fact; 'Describe' = say what happens in order; 'Explain' = give a reason using 'because' or 'so'; 'Compare' = similarities and differences together; 'Suggest' = apply knowledge to an unfamiliar situation.
**Use the exact words:** 'secrete', 'directly into the bloodstream', 'target organ', 'slower but acts for longer', 'master gland'. Missing one key word can lose the mark.
**Do not mix up systems:** nervous = electrical impulses along neurones; hormonal = chemicals in the blood.
**Check the diagram:** decide whether it shows a male or a female before naming ovaries or testes.

mistakes.r: Hormones are secreted directly into the bloodstream and carried in the blood to the target organ.
mistakes.w: Hormones travel along nerves to the target organ.

mistakes.r: The effects of hormones are slower but act for longer than nervous responses.
mistakes.w: The endocrine system is faster than the nervous system.

mistakes.r: A hormone only affects its target organ, whose cells have matching receptors.
mistakes.w: A hormone affects every cell it passes.

mistakes.r: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood, not through ducts.
mistakes.w: Glands release hormones through tubes into the organ.

mistakes.r: The pituitary gland is at the base of the brain and the thyroid gland is in the neck.
mistakes.w: The pituitary gland is in the neck / the thyroid is in the brain.

mistakes.r: The pituitary secretes several hormones that act on other glands to stimulate other hormones to be released.
mistakes.w: The master gland makes all the hormones in the body.

mistakes.r: The pancreas makes digestive enzymes and also hormones (insulin and glucagon) that control blood glucose.
mistakes.w: The pancreas only makes digestive enzymes.

mistakes.r: Adrenaline is made by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys.
mistakes.w: Adrenaline is made in the kidneys.

mistakes.r: Ovaries secrete oestrogen (and progesterone); testes secrete testosterone.
mistakes.w: The ovaries produce testosterone and the testes produce oestrogen.

mistakes.r: Nervous responses are fast and short-lived; hormonal responses are slower and longer-lasting.
mistakes.w: Nervous responses last longer than hormonal responses.

summary: AQA: you must know that the endocrine system is made up of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream, which carries each hormone to a target organ where it has its effect; that hormonal effects are slower but act for longer than nervous responses; that the pituitary gland is the 'master gland'; and you must identify the positions of the pituitary gland, pancreas, thyroid, adrenal gland, ovary and testes on a diagram of the body. It matters because it underpins blood glucose control, reproduction and negative feedback.

terms.d: A system of glands that secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream.
An organ that makes and releases a useful substance, for example a hormone.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland and carried in the blood to a target organ.
The blood flowing round the body, which carries hormones from glands to target organs.
The organ on which a hormone has its effect.
A molecule on or in a target cell with a shape that matches a particular hormone, allowing the cell to respond.
The 'master gland' at the base of the brain that secretes several hormones which act on other glands.
Another name for the pituitary gland, because its hormones stimulate other glands to release their hormones.
An organ below the stomach that secretes insulin and glucagon and also makes digestive enzymes.
A gland in the neck that secretes thyroxine.
A gland on top of each kidney that secretes adrenaline.
The female reproductive organ and endocrine gland that secretes oestrogen and progesterone.
The male reproductive organ and endocrine gland that secretes testosterone (plural: testes).
A hormone from the pancreas that helps to lower blood glucose concentration.
A hormone from the pancreas that helps to raise blood glucose concentration.
A hormone from the thyroid gland that stimulates the basal metabolic rate and is important for growth and development.
A hormone from the adrenal glands that prepares the body for flight or fight by increasing heart rate and boosting delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.
The main female reproductive hormone, secreted by the ovaries.
The main male reproductive hormone, secreted by the testes, which stimulates sperm production.
A hormone secreted by the pituitary gland that acts on the kidneys to control water content of the blood.

worked.ans: Model answer: The nervous system sends electrical impulses along neurones, whereas the endocrine system secretes chemical hormones into the bloodstream. Nervous responses are very fast and short-lived, whereas hormonal responses are slower but act for longer.
worked.q: Compare the way the nervous system and the endocrine system send information around the body. (4 marks)
steps: Mark 1: nervous system uses electrical impulses whereas the endocrine system uses chemical hormones.
Mark 2: nervous impulses travel along neurones whereas hormones are carried in the blood.
Mark 3: nervous responses are very fast whereas hormonal responses are slower.
Mark 4: nervous effects are short-lived whereas hormonal effects last longer.

worked.ans: The hormone is carried to all parts of the body in the blood, but only the target organ has matching receptors for the hormone. Other cells have no matching receptors, so only the target organ responds.
worked.q: Hormones are carried in the blood to all parts of the body, but each hormone only affects its target organ. Explain why. (3 marks)
steps: The blood carries the hormone around the whole body, so it reaches every organ.
The cells of the target organ have receptors with a shape that matches the hormone.
Cells in other organs do not have these receptors, so they do not respond.

worked.ans: Model answer: Nerve impulses travel quickly along neurones, causing the immediate reaction of jumping away. The adrenal glands secrete adrenaline into the blood, which increases the heart rate and boosts delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles. Hormonal effects are slower but last longer, so the heart keeps beating fast for several minutes.
worked.q: A boy sees a car coming towards him and jumps out of the way. His heart carries on beating very fast for several minutes. Explain how the nervous system and the endocrine system are involved. (4 marks)
steps: Nervous system: electrical impulses along neurones give a fast, immediate response (jumping out of the way).
Endocrine system: the adrenal glands secrete adrenaline into the blood.
Adrenaline increases the heart rate and boosts the delivery of oxygen and glucose to the brain and muscles.
Hormone effects are slower but act for longer, so the heart rate stays high for a while.
